subtopics.title: Report Basics and Scoring
subtopics.summary: The Global Gender Gap Report is an annual flagship publication of the World Economic Forum, introduced in 2006. It tracks how far countries have closed gender disparities rather than only counting women's absolute outcomes. Each country is scored from 0 to 1, and the scores are also expressed on a 0-100 scale where 100 means complete parity. The index is built on four dimensions.
facts: Introduced in 2006 by the World Economic Forum
The 2026 report is the 20th edition
Annual flagship publication of the World Economic Forum
Tracks closing of gender disparities, not women's absolute outcomes
Four dimensions: Economic Participation and Opportunity, Educational Attainment, Health and Survival, Political Empowerment
Score of 0 reflects absolute inequality; score of 1 means complete gender equality
Scores expressed on a 0-100 scale; 100 represents complete parity
World Economic Forum is a Switzerland-based think tank and advocacy group
The Forum was founded by Klaus Schwab in 1971

subtopics.title: Global Highlights and Leadership
subtopics.summary: Iceland retained the first position for the 17th consecutive year, while Chad ranked last among 145 countries. The world has closed 69.2% of the overall gender gap, improving by only 0.4 percentage points in the year. At the current pace, complete parity could take about 120 years. Women hold 19.1% of CEO positions globally.

subtopics.title: India's Performance
subtopics.summary: India retained its 131st position among 145 countries, with an overall gender parity score of 64.5%. Its dimension scores are 96.6% in educational attainment, 95.6% in health and survival, 41.2% in economic participation and opportunity, and 24.5% in political empowerment. Women hold only 5.9% of ministers and 13.1% of senior leadership and managerial positions. The booklet notes that progress in education and health has not yet carried over to the economic and political dimensions.

subtopics.title: Barriers and Government Initiatives
subtopics.summary: Women spend nearly five hours a day on unpaid household chores, three times more than men, and this unpaid work is valued at 22.7 lakh crore or 7.5% of GDP. Labour market, workplace safety and childcare issues continue to hinder women's participation. The Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam mandates 33% representation for women in legislatures. Schemes such as Beti Bachao Beti Padhao, PM Matru Vandana Yojana and Pradhan Mantri Jan-Dhan Yojana support girls' education, maternal health and financial access.

quizzes.passage: The Global Gender Gap Index is an annual flagship publication of the World Economic Forum. It tracks the extent to which countries have closed gender disparities, rather than simply measuring women's absolute outcomes. The index has four dimensions: economic participation and opportunity, educational attainment, health and survival, and political empowerment. Each nation is scored from 0 to 1, and the scores are expressed on a 0-100 scale, where 100 represents complete parity. In the 2026 report, India retained its position in the rankings. Its performance is uneven across the dimensions. In educational attainment and in health and survival, India's scores are close to complete parity, and the booklet describes near-complete parity between boys and girls in secondary and tertiary enrolment. Economic participation and political empowerment show far wider gaps. Women are a small share of ministers and of members of the Lok Sabha, and they hold a limited share of senior leadership and managerial posts. In corporate India, women are also few among chief executives and board members. The booklet notes that progress in education and health has not yet carried over to the economic and political dimensions. The booklet also notes that women's share among professional and technical workers has increased, even as women remain under-represented in senior roles. Overall, the booklet presents India's gender gap as a mix of strong and weak dimensions.

quizzes.passage: India's overall gender parity score in the 2026 report is 64.5%, and the booklet compares it with a global average. The country's performance differs sharply across the four dimensions. Education is its strongest area, and the booklet says India has attained near-complete parity between boys and girls in secondary and tertiary enrolment. Health and survival is also close to parity. Economic participation and political empowerment are much weaker. Women's share among professional and technical workers has nearly doubled since 2006, which shows some progress in the workforce. However, few women reach the top. The booklet notes low representation in leadership, with few women among chief executives and board members in Indian corporates. In the political sphere, women hold a small share of seats in the Lok Sabha, and their share of ministers has fallen from an earlier peak. Among the booklet's figures for the workforce, women hold a notable share of professional roles, but few hold the most senior positions. Women are also underrepresented in senior leadership and managerial positions. The booklet notes that gains in education and health have not yet translated into the economic and political dimensions. In the Lok Sabha, women's share in 2024 is below their share in 2019. The overall picture is one of progress in some areas and persistent gaps in others.

quizzes.passage: Women's participation in India's labour market has risen between 2017-18 and 2023-24, but much of their work remains in informal, low-paid roles. Workplace safety concerns and inadequate childcare are among the major hurdles they face. Women also carry a heavy load of unpaid domestic work, and the booklet puts a value on this work in economic terms. Girls' education faces obstacles too. A considerable share of girls aged 15 to 18 are not in school, and many drop out because of a lack of hygiene infrastructure and societal stigma. Female literacy also trails male literacy. Government programmes respond to these gaps by supporting girls' education, maternal health and women's access to financial services. Maternal health programmes have contributed to a fall in maternal mortality, and the National Health Mission aims to deliver affordable, quality healthcare to India's most vulnerable. The booklet also notes that many government programmes face setbacks due to poor outreach, lack of awareness and weak execution, especially in remote and rural areas. Constitutional provisions also address women's representation in legislatures. The booklet lists these challenges in its section on barriers to gender equality in India. In the education system, female literacy is set against male literacy as one of the gaps the booklet highlights. The booklet describes participation as rising despite most women remaining in informal, low-paid roles.

quizzes.passage: Several programmes aim to improve outcomes for girls and women. Beti Bachao Beti Padhao targets the falling child sex ratio and champions girls' survival, safety and schooling. Vigyan Jyoti is a flagship scheme that empowers meritorious schoolgirls to shine in STEM fields. Pradhan Mantri Jan-Dhan Yojana supports women's autonomy through financial access, and women have opened large numbers of bank accounts under it. The National Health Mission aims to deliver affordable, quality healthcare to India's most vulnerable. Pradhan Mantri Matru Vandana Yojana offers maternity benefits to pregnant and lactating women across India. Maternal health programmes have reduced the maternal mortality rate. Unpaid work is another part of the picture. Women spend many hours each day on household chores, and the booklet estimates the economic value of this unpaid work in lakh crore. Female literacy remains lower than male literacy, and a large share of girls in the 15 to 18 age group are outside school. Despite rising participation, most women remain in informal, low-paid work. Workplace safety concerns and inadequate childcare remain major hurdles for women at work. The Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam mandates representation for women in legislatures. The booklet also notes that many government programmes face setbacks due to poor outreach and weak execution, especially in remote and rural areas.
